name: Kaiming Liu
title: Physics PhD student
description: Kaiming Liu is a Physics PhD student at UIUC studying scientific machine learning, inverse problems, and simulation-to-experiment robustness.
bio: My research focuses on scientific machine learning and inverse problems: inferring physical models from measurements, representing uncertainty, and checking inferred parameters against the underlying physics.

Before moving to computational research, I studied thin-film materials using molecular beam epitaxy and scanning tunneling microscopy. That experimental background shapes my interest in methods that remain useful when simulations meet noisy, imperfect measurements.

research.title: Probabilistic inference for physical models
research.text: I study crystal electric field (CEF) inverse problems, where different model parameters can explain similar observations. My current work explores multimodal parameter inference and physics-based forward reconstruction to assess which solutions are consistent with the measurements.

research.title: From simulation to experiment
research.text: I investigate how inference methods trained on simulated data respond to experimental noise and distribution shift. The aim is to understand when an inferred model can be trusted, with applications to magnetic and scattering inverse problems.

research.title: Computational many-body physics
research.text: My computational background also includes neural-network backflow wavefunctions and variational Monte Carlo for strongly correlated fermions, with an emphasis on numerical implementation, sampling, and reproducible computation.

background: In Vidya Madhavan’s group at UIUC, I grew thin-film heterostructures with MBE, used STM/STS in ultrahigh vacuum, and developed temperature-control and data-analysis tools. Earlier research included Rydberg-atom simulations at Xi’an Jiaotong University and STM research in Michael F. Crommie’s group at UC Berkeley.
interests: Scientific machine learning; inverse problems; probabilistic and multimodal inference; physics-based forward validation; simulation-to-experiment transfer; computational condensed matter physics.

education.degree: Special Class for the Gifted Young

experience.role: Graduate research, Bryan K. Clark group
bullets: Develop probabilistic approaches to crystal electric field inverse problems, including multimodal parameter inference and reconstruction of observables with physics-based forward models.
Study the sensitivity of scientific inference to experimental noise and simulation-to-experiment distribution shift, with applications to magnetic and scattering models.
Implemented neural-network backflow wavefunctions for strongly correlated fermionic systems and ran variational Monte Carlo simulations with parallel sampling on computing clusters.
Profiled sampling, local-energy evaluation, and optimization stages; refactored sampling routines to reuse wavefunction evaluations.
Grew thin-film heterostructures by molecular beam epitaxy and characterized materials using STM/STS in ultrahigh-vacuum systems.
Built an automated MBE temperature-control program with feedback loops, measurement logging, and alerts to support repeatable growth protocols.
Developed Python and MATLAB analysis routines for STM/STS data, including constant-energy contour extraction and joint-density-of-states calculations for quasiparticle-interference studies.
Simulated Rydberg-atom dynamics and photon-mediated interactions with MATLAB and Python to study quantum nonlinear optics.
Built a discrete-time lattice simulation to examine two-qubit phase-flip dynamics and explore many-body regimes.

experience.role: Research assistant, Michael F. Crommie group
bullets: Assisted with synthesis and STM characterization of graphene nanoribbons containing five-membered rings, supporting studies of their electronic states.

teaching.text: Led discussion and laboratory sections, held office hours, and provided feedback on assignments in electromagnetism and modern physics.
